title: What Have I Left to Give, My Life Already Given?...
text:
What have I left to give, my life already given?

If seed, scattered into another furrow,

if sap, spilled over every soil,

if flame, burned in every vessel of darkness.


What have I left to give, my death

as well? In every dream, in every day;

my vertical death, my deaf death

that no one knows yet belongs to me.


What have I left to give, if in giving I give

-and because it is mine, and from now on

if God does not hold me back or cut off

my clumsy hands- my resurrection...!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's escalating gift-language, ending in resurrection as the last thing left to give.

title: Song to the Sterile Woman
text:
Impossible mother: blinded well, broken amphora,

submerged cathedral...

Water above you... and salt. And the remote

sunlight that never quite reaches you. Life

does not pass from your breast; in you Life strikes

and rebounds, then leaves diverted, lost,

to one side-to one side...

Toward where?...

Like Night, you pass over the earth

leaving no traces

of your shadow; and to the bloodied cry

of Life, your life does not answer,

deaf with the divine deafness of the stars...
editorial_note: The translation preserves the historical title and the cosmic imagery while keeping the voice elegiac rather than clinical.

title: The Last Hour
text:
Compelled by miserable cynicism,

Judas is there at that supper,

and though he restrains envy and fear,

he lowers his bewildered eyes.


Christ, withdrawn into his dreams,

and with a word full of sweetness,

without anger says, in serene calm:

"One who is here has betrayed me!"


Then the apostles trembled;

looking at one another in fear, they wavered...

and Peter, rising, cried:


"Say which of us is guilty,

so I may spit in the wretch's face!"

And Christ said nothing. He smiled.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sonnet's dramatic contrast between Peter's fury and Christ's silent smile.

title: May God Rot the Tongue That Moves Against You!
text:
May God rot the tongue of whoever moves it

against you; may he nail stiff to a wall

the arm that dares

to point at you; the dark cave-hand

that drops one more drop of vinegar into your thirst!...

Those who want you to serve for what

other women serve for

do not know that you are

Eve...

Eve without curse,

white and sleeping Eve

in a garden of flowers, in a forest of fragrance!

They do not know that you keep the key to a life!...

They do not know that you are the trembling mother

of a child who calls you from the Sun!...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the fierce protective curse and the poem's recasting of the addressee as an unfallen Eve.

title: The Whole World Has Been Left Empty to Me...
text:
The whole world has been left empty to me, abandoned by the

men who forgot to take me with them.

I am alone on this vast earth, with no company but the

animals the men do not need either, and the trees

they do not think they need.

And tomorrow, when they lack the lark's song or the perfume

of the rose, they will remember that there was a flower and that there was a

bird. And perhaps they will think it was good to have them.

But when they lack my timid verse, no one will know that once

I walked among them.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the prose-poem movement from human abandonment to the future absence of the poet's own verse.
